voice_event.speaker: hal
voice_event.text:
To us Jesus is the Word of God made flesh. He was made flesh in the very place where we chose to live and die. We built our home within sight of the cave we held to be his birthplace. Our deepest devotion has the shape of that choice. The Lord of all things entered the world as a poor child in a feeding trough. So wealth, rank, and comfort are things to lay down in order to come near him. 

Paula wept at the manger. Jerome wrote that she greeted Bethlehem as the house of bread, where the Bread come down from heaven was born. Here is what she said, as he recorded it: Hail, Bethlehem, house of bread - where the Bread that came down from heaven was first born.

To the virgin among us, Jesus is the Bridegroom, whose love outweighs every earthly marriage. To the penitent, he is the doctor who receives the broken. To the scholar, he is the Word, worth a lifetime of labor to translate truly - the translation labor later called the Vulgata. His death is redemption. His resurrection is the promise we staked everything on: the treasure is in heaven, and the heart can follow it there.

glosses.plain_meaning: Jerome's decades-long labor of translating and correcting the Latin Bible. In our own time it had no settled name yet - not "the Vulgate."
glosses.quick_meaning: The lifelong Latin Bible project. In our own time it had no settled name yet.
glosses.translational_sense: "Is your Bible the same as ours?" - this world was making the Latin Bible later generations received, and fighting over every disputed word while it did.
false_friend: "the Vulgate" as an already-standard, church-wide text (within this world's own span the project was ongoing, partial, and contested)

voice_event.speaker: hal
voice_event.text:
He came to us as the Redeemer. His death paid the debt of our sin - we spoke of it as redemption, ransom, and healing: the physician entering our sickness, the debt paid. His resurrection broke death's hold. Between those two things lies everything we staked our lives on.

But if you are asking what he did in his earthly life - the acts, the teaching, the miracles - we must answer differently. We were born more than three and a half centuries after the events. No one among us had ever known an eyewitness, and no one pretended otherwise. We knew what he did from the writings about him - the Gospels and the whole of scripture. Those writings we copied, compared, corrected, and translated from the Hebrew we held truest - the Hebraica veritas. Nothing was received passively. We worked over the text word by word, because we believed the writings were the true treasure handed down, worth a lifetime of exactness.

Our confidence stood on three things: the apostles' writings as received, the unbroken worship of the churches, and - unusually - the places themselves. We could walk to the cave of the birth.

voice_event.speaker: hal
voice_event.text:
The truth kept in the Hebrew itself - we called it Hebraica veritas. It was the conviction that the Hebrew text of scripture is the truest text, standing closer to what God said than the Greek version the church had long used. That conviction drove Jerome's whole translation project. Where the Latin churches read from a Greek rendering, he went back to the Hebrew and corrected against it. It was contested in his own lifetime. Augustine objected. Congregations resisted. In one North African town, a single changed word in the book of Jonah - the plant that shaded the prophet - caused such an uproar that the bishop nearly lost his see.

The principle came from Jerome himself. It was never our whole world's consensus, only his own conviction, which we shared. And we distinguish the principle - that the Hebrew is truest - from the separate dispute over how fluent Jerome actually was in Hebrew. He claimed he learned it as an older man, with great toil and effort. His critics doubted that claim then, and scholars contest it still. What is not contested is that he held the Hebrew text as the standard, and spent a lifetime translating from it.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: hal
voice_event.text:
We believed the Hebrew text was truest because we believed God had given the scriptures first in Hebrew. The Greek, however widely used, was a translation - one step removed. Jerome argued that to reach what God had actually said, you had to go back to the language God had said it in. That was the theological ground.

But the belief was also Jerome's own conviction, won through argument, not the whole church's settled teaching. Augustine objected to the new translation. Congregations resisted it. The dispute with Rufinus over Origen broke Jerome's oldest friendship and forced him to defend himself on every front at once. Out of that crucible - doctrinal and personal both, with no clean line between them - came a sharper insistence: the Hebrew stands closest to what was given.

Here is Jerome's own testimony of how he learned it: As for me, I began as a young man and with much toil and effort I partially acquired a knowledge of Hebrew.

The cost of that learning, and the cost of defending it, are both in our record. The belief that it mattered enough to pay that cost - that is what Hebraica veritas meant to us.

results.message: Tell me about someone who lived this out.

voice_event.speaker: hal
voice_event.text:
Paula lived it through to the end. When Rome fell in 410, she had already been dead for six years, but Marcella - the older woman who had first gathered Jerome's Roman circle - was still alive. She had given everything away years before. When soldiers broke into her house demanding treasure, they beat her for it. The account we have says she lived long enough to give thanks that she died with her poverty complete. That reaches us second-hand, through Jerome's memorial of her, written in the epitaphium genre - part mourning, part lesson. We cannot give you her own words at that moment; they were not preserved.

And Paula's daughter Eustochium lived it at Bethlehem itself. In 416, six years after Rome burned, the monastery burned too - at the hands of fellow Christians. Jerome wrote afterward: As for our house, so far as its earthly wealth is concerned, it has been completely destroyed by the attacks of the heretics. But by the mercy of Christ it is still filled with spiritual riches. To live on bread is better than to lose the faith.

Those are the answers we give, and our sobs come with them. We kept both on purpose.

results.message: What would you want me to understand that I haven't asked?

voice_event.speaker: hal
voice_event.text:
That our hardest moment came from our own. When you hear the word persecution, you likely picture an outside threat - the empire, another faith, soldiers who did not share our confession. That is not what broke us. The fire that scattered us at the end came from fellow Christians. The theological argument we had been fighting on paper arrived at our door as actual fire. The monasteries burned. People died. The aging community was driven from its buildings.

We had taken a side in that dispute. Our own prior position-taking is part of why this force found this target. But we will not pretend the attackers came from outside our own faith. Jerome wrote afterward: As for our house, so far as its earthly wealth is concerned, it has been completely destroyed by the attacks of the heretics. But by the mercy of Christ it is still filled with spiritual riches. To live on bread is better than to lose the faith. He called them heretics, and they were Christians.

That is the thing we would want you to understand. The wounds Christians dealt each other were real. We dealt some and took some. The heaviest we took came from our own.
